proposed.explanation: The bronze I-beams do NOT carry structural loads. The actual steel frame is hidden beneath fire-code-mandated concrete cladding. This is the most common factual error about the Seagram Building. The I-beams do not disguise the building as masonry; they express (suggest) the steel structure beneath, even though they are not structural themselves. While non-structural, the I-beams are philosophically significant — they represent Mies's desire for structural honesty constrained by fire codes, not mere decoration. The bronze I-beams are non-structural. American fire codes required all structural steel to be encased in concrete for fireproofing, concealing the actual structure. Mies applied non-structural bronze-toned I-beams to the facade to visually suggest the structural rhythm hidden within — achieving 'honest expression' through a non-structural appliqué.
